kurals.tamil:
அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும் ஒருவன்
புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Arangooraan alla seyinum oruvan,
Purangooraan endral inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Even if a man never speaks a word in praise of virtue and does nothing but wrong, it is still something good if people can say of him, “At least he does not speak ill of others behind their backs.”
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who forgets his homework, is messy, and gets into trouble a lot. But everyone says, “He never talks badly about anyone when they’re not around.” That one good thing still shines. This kural says not gossiping about people behind their backs is so important that even someone with lots of faults earns a little praise for it.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately provocative concession: he imagines a man who neither professes aram (virtue) nor practises it, and still finds one thing worth saying in his favour — that he is not a backbiter (puṟaṅkūṟāṉ, literally “one who speaks at the back”). The rhetorical move establishes a hierarchy of vices before any argument is made: slander is placed so low that merely abstaining from it counts as a redeeming trait. The verb “enṟal” (“that it be said”) is significant; the good in question is reputational, located in what the community can truthfully say of the man, which neatly mirrors the fact that backbiting is itself a crime against another’s reputation. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read the couplet as an argument a fortiori: if non-slander redeems even the unrighteous, how much more is it required of the righteous. The chapter sits in the householder section (Illaraviyal) right after Envy and Covetousness, reflecting a sequence from inner vices to their expression in speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…non-violence, truthfulness, absence of anger, renunciation, peacefulness, restraint from fault-finding, compassion toward all living beings…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the qualities of a divine nature, and one of them is apaiśunam — literally “non-paiśunya,” refraining from slander and fault-finding about others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita counts not backbiting as a core mark of a good person; the Kural says it is so basic that even a bad person gets credit for it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Apaiśunam is the direct Sanskrit counterpart of puṟaṅkūṟāmai; the Gita lists it among virtues but does not make the Kural’s ‘even a sinner’ argument.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law”
christianity.explanation: James tells the early Christians flatly not to speak against each other, because running someone down makes you a judge in God’s place.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat speaking evil of others as a stand-alone wrong serious enough to be named on its own.
christianity._accuracy_note: Direct prohibition of evil-speaking; lacks the Kural’s comparative framing about the otherwise sinful man.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not spy or backbite each other. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids ghībah (backbiting) and compares it to eating your dead brother’s flesh — attacking someone who cannot defend himself because he is not there.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an and the Kural both single out speaking about someone behind his back as a uniquely ugly act.
islam._accuracy_note: Ghībah is almost exactly puṟaṅkūṟal; the Qur’an’s image stresses the victim’s absence just as the Tamil word does.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s command against being a rakhil (talebearer) is the root of the whole Jewish law of lashon hara, harmful speech about others.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Torah treats carrying tales about others as its own named commandment, set right beside protecting a neighbour’s life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct scriptural ban on talebearing; the Kural’s ‘even if he does evil’ concession has no parallel here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is right speech? Abstaining from lying, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from abusive speech, abstaining from idle chatter: This, monks, is called right speech.”
buddhism.explanation: In defining the Eightfold Path, the Buddha makes avoiding divisive speech (pisuṇā vācā, tale-bearing) one of the four parts of Right Speech.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism, like the Kural, puts refusing to talk others down at the foundation of ethical life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Pisuṇā vācā overlaps strongly with backbiting; the sutta is a definition rather than a ranking of vices.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not get a name either as lavish or as churlish; as a friend of rogues or as a slanderer of good men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farmer-wisdom warns his brother to guard his reputation, and one of the worst names a man can earn is ‘slanderer of good men.’
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod and Valluvar both frame the issue in terms of what people say of you: being known as a non-slanderer is itself a good name.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on the reputational angle (‘enṟal’ — what is said of a man); Hesiod is gnomic poetry rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We may, however, enter, though sparingly, into discourse sometimes when occasion calls for it, but not on any of the common subjects … but principally not of men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons.”
philosophy.explanation: In his rules for everyday conduct, Epictetus tells the student that talking about other people, and above all finding fault with them, is the first kind of conversation to give up.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar picks out the same habit as the one to drop first, so much so that someone who manages only this much has still done something good.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 33 (tr. Elizabeth Carter (as edited at the Internet Classics Archive))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter). Strong on refraining from blaming people in speech; Epictetus does not single out speaking behind someone's back, nor make the Kural's 'at least he does this' concession.

kurals.tamil:
அறனழீஇ அல்லவை செய்தலின் தீதே
புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranazheei allavai seydhalin theedhe,
Puranazheeip poiththu nagai.
kurals.meaning: To tear a person down behind his back and then smile falsely at him to his face is worse than openly rejecting virtue and doing evil.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a classmate says mean things about you when you’re gone, then comes up and grins at you like your best friend. That’s worse than someone who is just openly naughty — because the fake smile is a trick. This kural says the two-faced person is worse than the openly bad one.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a pointed parallelism: aṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying virtue”) against puṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying [someone] at the back”), with the second judged worse (tītē). What tips the scale is the final phrase poyttu nakai, “smiling falsely” — the backbiter compounds slander with a feigned intimacy in the victim’s presence. Valluvar is thus condemning not only malicious speech but hypocrisy as a structure of relationship, a split between the face and the back that corrupts the trust on which the householder’s social world rests. The claim that this is worse than open wickedness anticipates a widely shared intuition across ethical traditions: the open enemy can be guarded against, but the smiling detractor disarms his victim first. The verse also sharpens 181: there, abstaining from slander redeemed a sinner; here, slander joined to false friendliness sinks a man below the sinner.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Parth, the qualities of those who possess a demoniac nature are hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names dambha — hypocrisy, showing a good face while hiding a bad heart — as the very first mark of a demonic nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts rank the false face above open vice; the smiling backbiter of the Kural is a textbook case of dambha.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Hypocrisy matches the ‘false smile’ element; the Gita does not speak of slander specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist laments a companion who spoke sweetly to his face while plotting against him.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s smiling backbiter exactly: soft speech in front, a drawn sword behind.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-exact portrait of the two-faced friend; the Kural’s comparative claim (‘worse than open evil’) is implicit, not stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “The worst people in the Sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection will be the double faced people who appear to some people with one face and to other people with another face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet calls the two-faced person (dhu’l-wajhayn) the worst of people before God.
islam.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the hadith ranks the double-faced person at the very bottom — below other kinds of sinners.
islam._accuracy_note: Both the two-facedness and the superlative ranking (‘worst people’) match the Kural closely.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Their tongue is a sharpened arrow; it speaks deceit. One speaks peaceably to his neighbor with his mouth, but in his heart he lies in wait for him”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud’s discussion of malicious speech quotes Jeremiah’s picture of the peaceful-mouthed ambusher, and in the same passage the school of Rabbi Yishmael says lashon hara outweighs idolatry, sexual sin, and bloodshed combined.
judaism.tie_back: Both the ranking (worse than the gravest sins) and the peaceful face over a hidden attack match the Kural’s verdict.
judaism._accuracy_note: Two-faced speech plus an explicit ‘worse than the cardinal sins’ ranking — a strong double match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who flatters be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he approves of his friend's evil deeds, (ii) he disapproves his friend's good deeds, (iii) he praises him in his presence, (iv) he speaks ill of him in his absence.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches the layman Sigala to recognise the false friend: praise to your face, slander behind your back.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s ‘foe in the guise of a friend’ is the Kural’s backbiter who smiles falsely — almost word for word.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Nearly one-to-one: praise in presence, ill-speech in absence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For hateful in my eyes, even as the gates of Hades, is that man that hideth one thing in his mind and sayeth another.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles rebuffs Agamemnon’s envoys, declaring that he loathes a man who says one thing and hides another in his heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles and Valluvar share a special loathing for the split between the face and the heart.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures the duplicity; Achilles is speaking of deceit in general, not slander in particular.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But of all forms of injustice, none is more flagrant than that of the hypocrite who, at the very moment when he is most false, makes it his business to appear virtuous.”
philosophy.explanation: Having said that wrong is done either by force or by fraud and that fraud is the more contemptible, Cicero ranks the hypocrite who wears a mask of goodness while deceiving as the worst wrongdoer of all.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Cicero says the false friendly face is worse than open wrongdoing.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book I, §41 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis I.20-41, Miller). Very close on the ranking (hypocrisy worse than open wrong); Cicero speaks of hypocrisy generally rather than slander behind someone's back specifically.

kurals.tamil:
புறங்கூறிப் பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்
அறங்கூற்றும் ஆக்கத் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Purangoorip poiththuyir vaazhdhalin saadhal,
Arangootrum aakkath tharum.
kurals.meaning: Rather than staying alive by backbiting people and being false to their faces, it is better to die; death brings the true gain that the teachings of virtue speak of.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you could stay popular only by telling mean secrets about your friends and pretending to be nice to them. This kural says it’s better to lose everything than to live that way — being a good, honest person matters more than anything you could win by gossip.
kurals.university: The couplet raises the stakes from comparison of vices to a comparison between a way of life and death itself. Puṟaṅkūṟip poyttu uyir vāḻtal — “living by backbiting and falsehood” — names a whole livelihood, the courtier’s or social climber’s art of advancing by undermining others. Against this Valluvar sets cātal, death, which paradoxically yields ākkam (prosperity, gain) of the kind that aṟam-kūṟṟu, the pronouncements of the moral treatises, recognise. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss the death as dying in poverty for having refused such conduct — a reading that turns the verse into a choice between material survival bought by slander and moral gain secured by refusing it. The structure echoes a theme found across classical ethics: that there are lives not worth living, and that moral ruin is a worse fate than death.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that for an honourable person, living on in disgrace is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say a dishonourable life is worse than death; the Kural names backbiting as one such dishonourable life.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘death over dishonour’ logic; the Gita’s context is cowardice in battle, not slander.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters … they which commit such things are worthy of death”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists backbiters among those whose deeds, by God’s judgment, deserve death.
christianity.tie_back: Paul names backbiting specifically and links it to death; the Kural too weighs a backbiter’s life against death.
christianity._accuracy_note: Topical match (backbiters, death) but the logic differs: Paul pronounces judgment; Valluvar says an honest death is preferable to such a life.

islam.quote_or_event: “one of them never saved himself from being soiled with his urine while the other used to go about with calumnies (to make enmity between friends).”
islam.explanation: Passing two graves, the Prophet revealed that one man was being punished after death for spreading tales (namīmah) that set friends against each other.
islam.tie_back: The hadith shows that a life lived by slander carries its cost beyond death — the Kural’s point that such a life is not worth its gains.
islam._accuracy_note: Shows the gravity of tale-bearing in light of death; does not make the Kural’s ‘better to die than live so’ comparison.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Third speech, i.e., malicious speech about a third party, kills three people. It kills the one who speaks malicious speech, and the one who accepts the malicious speech when he hears it, and the one about whom the malicious speech is said.”
judaism.explanation: The Sages of the Land of Israel taught that backbiting is lethal — even to the one who speaks it.
judaism.tie_back: If slander ‘kills’ the slanderer, then, as the Kural says, living by it is already a kind of death, worse than an honest one.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic link between slander and death; the preference for literal death is the Kural’s own twist.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy is life for the shameless one who is impudent as a crow, is backbiting and forward, arrogant and corrupt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada notes that the backbiter’s life is easy, while the next verse says the modest, pure life is hard.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts admit slander can make life easier — and both say that easy life is the wrong one to choose.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Explicitly names backbiting as a way to an easy life to be rejected; does not mention death.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ajax, shamed after his madness, tells his wife Tecmessa that a man of noble birth must either live with honour or die with honour, and then takes his own life rather than live disgraced.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles’ tragic hero decides that a dishonourable life is not worth keeping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ajax embodies the Kural’s ‘death is better than a base life,’ though his disgrace comes from madness, not slander.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: shares the honour-over-life principle only; no slander involved, and the Kural does not endorse suicide. Paraphrased, not quoted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.”
philosophy.explanation: Condemned to die, Socrates tells the jury that wrongdoing is the real danger to flee, not death.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and Valluvar agree: death is a lesser evil than living by injustice such as slander and falsehood.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close structural match (death vs. moral ruin); Socrates speaks of injustice generally, and was himself a victim of slander.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும் சொல்லற்க
முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannindru kannarach chollinum sollarka,
Munnindru pinnokkaach chol.
kurals.meaning: You may even speak harshly and without kindness to a person’s face, but never speak words behind his back without thinking about the harm they will cause.
kurals.elementary: If your friend does something wrong, it’s okay to tell them straight to their face, even if it’s hard to hear. What’s not okay is saying it to others when your friend isn’t there. Say it to their face or don’t say it at all.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a set of spatial and visual puns. Kaṇ niṉṟu (“standing before the eyes”) is paired with kaṇ aṟa (“with the eye cut off,” i.e., without kaṇṇōṭṭam, the courteous regard that Valluvar treats as a virtue in chapter 58), while muṉ niṉṟu (“having stood in front”) contrasts with piṉ nōkkā col, which carries two senses: words that do not look to consequences, and words aimed at someone’s back. Valluvar concedes a real cost — harsh, face-to-face speech is not ideal — but ranks it clearly above secret disparagement, because direct speech leaves the target free to answer, correct, or defend himself. This makes the verse a procedural ethic of speech: criticism is legitimate in principle, but its moral character depends on the presence of the person criticised. The same structure appears in legal ideals of hearing both parties and in religious norms of private, direct rebuke.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the discipline of speech as saying what is true and beneficial without needlessly upsetting others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s standard of true and beneficial speech rules out consequence-blind talk behind someone’s back, which is exactly what the Kural forbids.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General ethic of speech; does not address the face vs. behind-the-back distinction that defines this kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to take a grievance straight to the person, privately, before involving anyone else.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus, like Valluvar, says to tell a person’s fault to his face rather than to others behind his back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on direct confrontation over talking behind the back; Jesus adds privacy and reconciliation as goals.

islam.quote_or_event: “Backbiting implies your talking about your brother in a manner which he does not like.” … “If (that failing) is actually found (in him) what you assert, you in fact backbited him, and if that is not in him it is a slander.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that talking about someone in a way he would dislike is ghībah even when it is true; if false, it is worse — slander.
islam.tie_back: Both texts agree that even true criticism becomes a wrong when it is spoken about the person rather than to him.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures ‘even true words’ being forbidden; the face-to-face alternative is implied rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Any statement that is said in the presence of its master, i.e., if the subject of the statement was there, does not have any prohibition due to malicious speech.”
judaism.explanation: Rabba rules that speech said in the subject’s presence is not lashon hara, citing Rabbi Yosei, who never said anything he would not say to the person himself; Abaye disagrees, calling it both impudence and lashon hara.
judaism.tie_back: Rabba’s rule is the Kural’s rule: saying it to someone’s face is a different and lesser matter than saying it behind his back.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match; note that Abaye’s dissenting view in the same passage treats face-to-face insult as still wrong — which also fits Valluvar’s ‘even harsh.’

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be factual, true, beneficial, but unendearing & disagreeable to others, he has a sense of the proper time for saying them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha explains that he will say unpleasant truths when they are beneficial, choosing the right time — as he did openly about Devadatta.
buddhism.tie_back: Both allow hard words spoken openly and for a purpose, while ruling out careless words that ignore consequences.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the permission for harsh-but-honest speech and the concern for consequences; the ‘behind the back’ contrast is not explicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “needs must I verily speak my word outright, even as I am minded, and as it shall be brought to pass”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles tells Odysseus he will speak bluntly to his face, and goes on to say he hates a man who hides one thing and says another.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles chooses the harsh, open word over hidden speech — the very preference Valluvar states.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for ‘speak harshly to the face’; Achilles is refusing an offer, not declining to slander.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every such person is a skulker and a coward; he will not come into the open; he is an ambuscader shooting from a lurking-place”
philosophy.explanation: Lucian argues that the slanderer is a coward: an honest accuser makes his charge publicly and lets it be examined.
philosophy.tie_back: Lucian and Valluvar both say: if you have a charge, bring it into the open where the person can answer.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Direct match on open charge vs. hidden slander.

kurals.tamil:
அறஞ்சொல்லும் நெஞ்சத்தான் அன்மை புறஞ்சொல்லும்
புன்மையாற் காணப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranjollum nenjaththaan anmai puranjollum,
Punmaiyaal kaanap padum.
kurals.meaning: However much a man talks about virtue, the pettiness of his backbiting shows that his heart is not truly given to virtue.
kurals.elementary: Someone might always say, “Be kind! Be fair!” But if you hear them gossiping meanly about people when those people leave, you know they don’t really mean what they say. Gossip is like a window that lets you see what’s really inside a person.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar turns backbiting into evidence. The phrase aṟañ-collum neñcattāṉ — one whose heart speaks of virtue, or, as many commentators read it, one who merely talks virtue — sets up a contrast between profession and inner reality, and puṟañ-collum puṉmai (“the meanness of speaking at the back”) becomes the diagnostic sign that exposes the gap. The verse therefore makes slander not only a wrong but a symptom: a person’s habitual talk about the absent is a more reliable index of character than his public moralising. The idea that inner character leaks out through small, unguarded habits is common to many ethical traditions, and it sharpens the chapter’s treatment of hypocrisy begun in 182. Valluvar implicitly invites the listener to read people by what they say about others when those others are not present.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses of action but whose mind dwells on sense objects certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls a mithyācāra (pretender) anyone who shows outward restraint while his mind stays attached to what he claims to renounce.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts expose the one whose outward religiosity hides an unchanged inner self; the Kural names backbiting as the giveaway.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the outward-vs-inward theme; the Gita’s pretender is about sense-control, not speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain.”
christianity.explanation: James says an uncontrolled tongue shows that a person’s religion is empty, however devout he appears.
christianity.tie_back: James and Valluvar agree: the tongue reveals whether the claimed virtue is real.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: outward religiosity exposed by misuse of the tongue.

islam.quote_or_event: “O community of people, who believed by their tongue, and belief did not enter their hearts, do not back-bite Muslims, and do not search for their faults”
islam.explanation: The Prophet addresses backbiters as people whose faith is on their tongues but has not reached their hearts.
islam.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own claim: backbiting shows that professed virtue has not entered the heart.
islam._accuracy_note: Strikingly exact: tongue-only faith, empty heart, backbiting as the sign.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who speaks malicious speech is considered as though he denied the fundamental belief in God.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yohanan teaches that the one who speaks lashon hara, whatever he professes, is effectively a denier of God.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say slander cancels out religious profession and shows what the speaker really believes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in logic — slander reveals the absence of real faith; framed theologically rather than morally.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares someone who recites teachings without living them to a hired cowherd counting cattle that aren’t his.
buddhism.tie_back: Both expose the person who speaks virtue without owning it; the Kural finds the proof in backbiting.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches ‘talks virtue, lacks it’; does not identify slander as the revealing sign.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Momus, the god of fault-finding, criticised the maker of man for not setting a door or window in the human breast, so that people’s real thoughts could be seen.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the tale Lucian retells, the carping god wanted people’s hidden intentions made visible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar suggests there already is such a window: a person’s backbiting shows what his heart is really like.
greek_mythology.source: Lucian, Hermotimus 20 (paraphrase of the Momus fable)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematic link on revealing hidden character; paraphrased, not verbatim. Ironically, Momus is himself the archetypal fault-finder.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for the highest reach of injustice is, to be deemed just when you are not.”
philosophy.explanation: In Glaucon’s challenge in the Republic, the perfectly unjust man is the one who keeps a reputation for justice while being unjust.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato names the danger the Kural helps us detect: the person who seems virtuous but is not, whose backbiting gives him away.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Same appearance/reality gap; Plato poses it as a challenge to answer, not as a diagnosis through speech.

kurals.tamil:
பிறன்பழி கூறுவான் தன்பழி யுள்ளும்
திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Piranpazhi kooruvaan thanpazhi yullum,
Thirantherindhu koorap padum.
kurals.meaning: The one who spreads others’ faults will have his own faults hunted out, and the worst of them picked and told about him in turn.
kurals.elementary: If you tell everyone about your friend’s mistakes, soon people start looking for your mistakes too — and they’ll pick the most embarrassing ones to share. Gossip is like a boomerang: it comes back to hit you.
kurals.university: The couplet states a law of reciprocity in the economy of reputation. Piṟaṉ paḻi kūṟuvāṉ (“one who speaks another’s blame”) will find that taṉ paḻi uḷḷum (“even among his own blameworthy deeds”) the ones chosen with discernment (tiṟaṉ terintu) will be spoken of. The phrase tiṟaṉ terintu is sharp: people will not merely repeat his faults but select the most damaging, just as the backbiter selected and polished the faults of others. Valluvar therefore presents slander as self-defeating — by making fault-finding normal, the slanderer licenses the same treatment of himself. The passive kūṟappaṭum (“will be spoken”) leaves the agent unspecified, allowing both a social reading (others will retaliate) and a moral-causal one akin to karma. The idea that judgment returns in the same measure is widely shared across ethical traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As it does and acts, so it becomes; by doing good it becomes good, and by doing evil it becomes evil”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad states the law of karma: a person becomes what he does.
hinduism.tie_back: The slanderer who deals in faults becomes a man of faults — and, as the Kural says, is spoken of for them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General karmic reciprocity; the Kural’s specific social mechanism (faults exposed in turn) is not in the text.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that the standard you use to judge others will be used to judge you.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s boomerang: pick at others’ faults and your own will be picked at the same way.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close principle of reciprocal judgment.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed whoever tries to expose his Muslims brother’s secrets, Allah exposes his secrets wide open, even if he were in the depth of his house.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that whoever hunts for and exposes others’ hidden faults will have his own hidden faults exposed by God.
islam.tie_back: Almost the Kural itself: the exposer of others’ faults will see his own faults exposed.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one reciprocity of exposure; the hadith names God as the agent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What is the meaning of that which is written: ‘This shall be the law of the leper [metzora]’ … This means that this shall be the law of a defamer [motzi shem ra].”
judaism.explanation: Reish Lakish reads metzora (one afflicted with tzara’at) as motzi shem ra, a defamer: the one who hid behind secret speech is publicly marked for it.
judaism.tie_back: In both, the slanderer’s own disgrace becomes public — his hidden fault is put on display.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures the exposure-in-return idea through a wordplay; the mechanism is divine affliction, not social retaliation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever harasses an innocent man, a man pure, without blemish: The evil comes right back to the fool like fine dust thrown against the wind.”
buddhism.explanation: Said of the monk Kokālika, who slandered Sāriputta and Moggallāna and came to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: Slander thrown at others blows back on the slanderer — the Kural’s point in a vivid image.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Explicitly about a slanderer and the rebound of his words.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises restraint of speech because evil-speaking comes back as worse talk about oneself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s exact claim: speak ill of others and you will be spoken of worse.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Hesiod’s ‘worse spoken of’ even echoes the Kural’s choosing of the worst faults.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You look at the pimples of others when you yourselves are covered with a mass of sores”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca turns on the critics who mock philosophers’ faults, reminding them how much worse their own are.
philosophy.tie_back: The fault-finder invites a return inspection that shows his own, larger faults — as the Kural predicts.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Seneca performs the counter-exposure the Kural describes; the quote itself is closer to kural 190’s self-examination theme.

kurals.tamil:
பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் நகச்சொல்லி
நட்பாடல் தேற்றா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pagachchollik kelirp pirippar nagachcholli,
Natpaadal thetraa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who do not know how to build friendship through pleasant, cheerful talk will speak words that divide people, and drive apart even their own close friends and kin.
kurals.elementary: Some people know how to make friends by saying kind, fun things. Others only know how to say “Did you hear what she said about you?” — and that makes friends fight. This kural says people who can’t make friends with nice words end up breaking friendships with nasty ones.
kurals.university: The verse is built on the chiastic pair paka-c-colli (“speaking so as to split”) and naka-c-colli (“speaking so as to make [people] laugh/rejoice”). Valluvar diagnoses divisive speech as a failure of social skill as much as of morality: those who cannot tēṟṟu (be sure of, master) the art of naṭpāṭal, friendship-making through genial conversation, fall back on the easier currency of tale-bearing. The object kēḷir means kin or intimates, so the damage falls on the speaker’s own circle — Parimelazhagar notes they alienate even their friends from themselves. This connects the chapter to the book’s later treatment of friendship (naṭpu, chapters 79–83) and recalls the Buddhist category of pisuṇā vācā, speech that splits people apart. The couplet implies a positive programme: cultivate the speech that unites, and the temptation to divide loses its hold.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, the maid Manthara whispers to Queen Kaikeyi that Rama’s coronation will ruin her and her son Bharata, turning a queen who loved Rama into the cause of his exile.
hinduism.explanation: Manthara’s poisonous tale-bearing breaks apart a royal family that had been united and loving.
hinduism.tie_back: Manthara is the Kural’s divider: her words split kin who had no quarrel until she spoke.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative example of divisive speech splitting kin; paraphrased from the episode, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that a whisperer — a gossip — breaks up even the closest friends.
christianity.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: divisive whispering separates intimates.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on separating close friends.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not obey every worthless habitual swearer [And] scorner, going about with malicious gossip -”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against following the one who goes about spreading namīm — tale-bearing that sows discord.
islam.tie_back: Both texts point to the gossip who circulates tales between people as someone to reject.
islam._accuracy_note: Names malicious tale-bearing directly; does not spell out the breaking of friendships.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What is different and notable about a leper, that the Torah states: ‘He shall dwell alone; outside of the camp shall be his dwelling’? He replied: By speaking malicious speech he separated between husband and wife and between one person and another”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud explains that the slanderer is made to live alone because his words had separated spouses and friends.
judaism.tie_back: Both identify the slanderer as one who splits apart people who belong together — and who ends up alone.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: division of intimates, with isolation as a fitting consequence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What he has heard here he tells there to break those people apart from these people here. What he has heard there he tells here to break these people apart from those people there.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines divisive speech (pisuṇā vācā) as carrying tales back and forth to break people apart.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s ‘speaking to split’ — the canonical Buddhist description of it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact definitional match; the same sutta praises speech that creates concord, mirroring the Kural’s ‘speaking to delight.’

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But abhorred Strife bare painful Toil and Forgetfulness and Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings also, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod’s family tree of the gods, Eris (Strife) gives birth to Lying Words and Disputes along with violence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Myth places divisive, lying speech in the family of Strife; the Kural shows that kind of speech tearing friends apart.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mythic genealogy linking false speech and discord; not specific to breaking friendships.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Many are the friendships that have been cut short, many the households set by the ears, because slander has found ready credence.”
philosophy.explanation: Lucian opens his essay on slander by listing the friendships and families it has destroyed.
philosophy.tie_back: Lucian and Valluvar both describe slander as the force that tears apart friends and kin.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match; Lucian stresses the listener’s credulity as well as the slanderer.

kurals.tamil:
துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும் மரபினார்
என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunniyaar kutramum thootrum marabinaar,
Ennaikol ethilaar maattu.
kurals.meaning: If people make a habit of broadcasting the faults even of those closest to them, what won’t they do to strangers?
kurals.elementary: If someone spreads secrets about their own best friend, imagine what they’d say about you! This kural says: watch how people talk about their closest friends — that’s how they’ll treat everyone else.
kurals.university: The couplet argues a fortiori from intimacy. Tuṉṉiyār (“those who are close”) are the people whom affection, obligation, and self-interest should all protect; if the slanderer’s marapu (settled disposition, habit) leads him to tūṟṟu (scatter abroad, as chaff is winnowed) even their faults, then no restraint can be expected toward ētilār, those who are unconnected to him. The rhetorical question ennaikol (“what indeed?”) leaves the outcome to the listener’s imagination. Valluvar is making a practical point about trust: how a person speaks of his intimates is the best predictor of how he will treat everyone else. The verse also implies that backbiting is not an occasional lapse but a trait, marapu, which, once formed, spares no one.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the honest are always pained at speaking ill of others, so do the wicked always rejoice in doing the same thing.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala says this after King Dushyanta, her own husband, publicly reviles her as a lewd woman and denies their son.
hinduism.tie_back: The king who slanders his own wife and child shows the Kural’s point: one who defames his intimates will spare no one.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: The narrative shows reviling of the closest kin; the quoted line is a general contrast of honest and wicked speech.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.”
christianity.explanation: God rebukes the wicked man who slanders even his own brother.
christianity.tie_back: The same outrage as the Kural: slander aimed at the closest of kin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches ‘faults even of intimates’; lacks the ‘what then of strangers?’ inference.

islam.quote_or_event: “whoever screened a Muslim, Allah will screen him on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a Muslim is a brother to be protected, and that covering a brother’s faults earns God’s covering of one’s own.
islam.tie_back: Islam sets the opposite ideal: those close to you are owed concealment of their faults, not exposure.
islam._accuracy_note: Contrasting positive duty; does not address the intimates-vs-strangers argument.

judaism.quote_or_event: Miriam and Aaron spoke against their own brother Moses; Miriam was struck with tzara’at and shut outside the camp for seven days.
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s example of lashon hara is aimed at a sibling, and later tradition treats it as the model case of the sin.
judaism.tie_back: Even a prophetess who spoke against her own brother was punished, showing how serious it is to disparage intimates.
judaism._accuracy_note: Speech against a close relative is the core of the episode; the ‘what then of strangers’ logic is not in the text. Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a liar who has violated the one law (of truthfulness) who holds in scorn the hereafter, there is no evil that he cannot do.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that once a person abandons truthful speech, no evil is beyond him.
buddhism.tie_back: Both argue from one proven vice to unlimited danger: if he does this, what won’t he do?
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the escalating ‘what won’t he do’ reasoning; subject is lying rather than betraying intimates.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “paying this penalty, they say, for the shameful weakness he displayed in failing to keep a bridle on his lips, when admitted by gods, though he was but mortal, to share the honours of their feasts like one of them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus was welcomed to the gods’ own table and then betrayed their confidences with an unbridled tongue.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus fits the Kural’s type: one who exposes even those who took him into their inner circle.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Betrayal of intimates through the tongue; the myth concerns revealing secrets more than defaming faults.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “When he is sitting with others, he loves to criticise one who has just left the circle; nay, if he has found an occasion, he will not abstain from abusing his own relations.”
philosophy.explanation: Theophrastus sketches the Evil-Speaker, who attacks whoever has just left the room and does not spare his own family.
philosophy.tie_back: Theophrastus draws the Kural’s portrait exactly: a backbiter who spares not even his kin.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact character sketch: backbiting the absent and abusing one’s own relations.

kurals.tamil:
அறன்நோக்கி ஆற்றுங்கொல் வையம் புறன்நோக்கிப்
புன்சொல் உரைப்பான் பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Arannokki aatrungol vaiyam purannokkip,
Punsol uraippaan porai.
kurals.meaning: Is it only out of regard for virtue that the earth still bears the weight of the man who waits until someone is gone and then speaks mean words about him?
kurals.elementary: The ground holds up everyone who walks on it — good people and mean people. This kural jokes that the Earth must be very patient and kind to keep carrying a gossip who waits for people to leave so he can say nasty things about them.
kurals.university: The couplet is one of Valluvar’s sharpest ironies. Vaiyam, the earth, is imagined as a moral agent who bears (āṟṟu) the poṟai (burden, weight) of the slanderer, and the poet wonders whether it does so only aṟaṉ nōkki — out of regard for dharma, since bearing all beings is its duty. The mirrored phrases aṟaṉ nōkki and puṟaṉ nōkki are carefully placed: the earth looks toward virtue, while the slanderer looks toward the back, watching for his victim’s absence before he speaks puṉ col, base words. The image draws on the Indian idea of the earth as the patient bearer of all beings, whose forbearance (poṟai also means patience) contrasts with the slanderer’s impatience to wound. Valluvar thus makes the slanderer a dead weight on the world, tolerated only by a patience he does not deserve.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the Earth (Bhūmi), weighed down by the burden of wicked kings, takes the form of a cow and goes weeping to Brahmā to ask for relief.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu myth pictures the Earth as a patient mother who carries the weight of the wicked until it becomes too much.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image: the earth patiently bearing the slanderer’s weight, only out of dharma.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘burdened, patient Earth’ image; the Purana’s wicked are tyrant-kings, not slanderers. Paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to God’s patience, which sustains even the wicked, as the model for loving enemies.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts marvel at a forbearance that keeps supporting even those who don’t deserve it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘undeserved sustenance of the wicked’ idea; lacks the Kural’s irony toward slanderers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if Allah were to impose blame on the people for what they have earned, He would not leave upon the earth any creature. But He defers them for a specified term.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says only God’s forbearance keeps wrongdoers on the earth at all.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the wrongdoer stays on the earth only because of a patience he has not earned.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of the tolerated wrongdoer on earth; not specific to slander.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He and I cannot dwell together in the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Hisda, citing Mar Ukva, says God declares this about anyone who speaks lashon hara, reading Psalm 101:5.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud and the Kural are equally astonished that the world has room for the slanderer at all.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit (the slanderer does not belong in the world); the Talmud has God refuse him, while the Kural has the earth grudgingly bear him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as when people throw what is clean or unclean on the earth — feces, urine, saliva, pus, or blood — the earth is not horrified, humiliated, or disgusted by it”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Rahula to make his mind like the earth, which accepts whatever is thrown on it without disgust.
buddhism.tie_back: Both use the earth as the model of boundless forbearance; the Kural ironically applies it to carrying the slanderer.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared image of the all-bearing earth; the Buddha uses it for meditation, not moral satire.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the gods by means of Helen's loveliness embroiled Troy and Hellas, causing death thereby, that they might lighten mother Earth of the outrage done her by the increase of man's number.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollo explains that the Trojan War was sent to relieve Mother Earth of the weight of too many mortals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek myth, like the Kural, imagines the earth as burdened by humans who weigh on her.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Orestes (Apollo’s closing speech) (E. P. Coleridge)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘burdened Earth’ motif only; the burden is population, not wickedness or slander.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “falling upon that earth out of which my father collected the seed … which bears me when I tread on it and abuse it for so many purposes.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius reflects with gratitude on the earth that patiently bears him even as he misuses it.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts marvel at the earth’s endurance of those who abuse it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the patient-earth image; Marcus is grateful rather than ironic, and slander is not the subject.

kurals.tamil:
ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
தீதுண்டோ மன்னும் உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ethilaar kutrampol thankutrang kaankirpin,
Theedhundo mannum uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: If people could see their own faults as clearly as they see the faults of others, could any harm come to living beings?
kurals.elementary: It’s easy to notice when a friend makes a mistake, but hard to notice our own. If everyone checked their own mistakes as carefully as they check others’, there would be much less gossip — and much less trouble for everyone.
kurals.university: Valluvar closes the chapter by moving from prohibition to cure. The comparison ētilār kuṟṟampōl (“like the faults of strangers”) captures the ease and even pleasure with which we see others’ failings; if that same clear sight were turned on taṉ kuṟṟam, one’s own faults, the rhetorical question asks, would any harm (tītu) remain for mannum uyir — beings who endure, or, in some commentaries, the soul that persists? The logic is psychological: backbiting feeds on an asymmetry of attention, and self-examination removes both the motive and the moral standing for it. Mu. Karunanidhi’s gloss draws out the practical point — the habit of slander disappears and life becomes peaceful. The ending thus turns the chapter’s condemnation of the slanderer into a discipline for the reader, echoing a strikingly wide range of traditions that contrast the tiny flaw in others with the large one in oneself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thou seest, O king, the fault of others, even though they be as small as a mustard seed. But seeing, thou noticest not thy own faults even though they be as large as the Vilwa fruit.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala rebukes King Dushyanta, who slanders her while blind to his own wrong in denying her.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s exact image: others’ tiny faults seen, one’s own huge faults ignored.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the asymmetry of seeing faults.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus mocks the person who picks at a speck in someone else’s eye while ignoring a plank in his own.
christianity.tie_back: The same lesson as the Kural: look at your own faults as sharply as you look at others’.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of you looks at the mote in his brother's eye while forgetting the stump in his own eye.”
islam.explanation: Abu Hurayra warns against seeing a speck in a brother’s eye while forgetting the stump in one’s own.
islam.tie_back: Same imbalance of sight that the Kural asks us to correct.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close image; this is a Companion’s saying (mawqūf), not a Prophetic hadith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I would be surprised if there is anyone in this generation who can receive rebuke. Why? Because if the one rebuking says to him: Remove the splinter from between your eyes, … the other says to him: Remove the beam from between your eyes”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon laments that people tell a critic to deal with his own bigger faults first.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts note how differently we see small faults in others and large ones in ourselves.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same splinter/beam asymmetry; the Talmud’s concern is receiving rebuke rather than self-examination as a cure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one's own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another's faults, but hides one's own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says we winnow others’ faults like chaff in the wind while hiding our own.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact statement of the Kural’s point — and the winnowing image matches the Tamil tūṟṟu of kural 188.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Hence it is that men are quick to see the faults of others, and yet are often blind to their own failings.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aesop’s fable, every person carries two bags: a small one in front holding the neighbours’ faults and a large one behind holding their own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable explains the very blindness that the Kural asks us to overcome.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-exact match; Aesopic fable rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We have other men's vices before our eyes, and our own behind our backs.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says anger at other people grows from this lopsided vision, and gives the example of a father, worse than his son, who scolds the son for the very extravagance he once indulged in himself.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca names the same blindness as the Kural, and like Valluvar treats it as the root of the harm people do to one another.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Anger (De Ira), Book II, ch. 28 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Of Anger/Book II, Stewart). Near one-to-one match on the image and its moral consequence. Same idea as the Aesop fable in the Greek mythology slot, but from a separate philosophical source.
